Experiments cover held-in and nominally held-out tasks, original-versus-synthetic images, three dataset sizes, and removal of table-interpretation tasks. The results demonstrate substantial gains over the same Qwen2.5-VL backbone and an MMTab-trained baseline on many benchmarks.
The paper provides useful implementation information, including rendering software, fine-tuning hyperparameters, input limits, compute usage, task prompts, and per-task dataset statistics.

The authors appropriately acknowledge several limitations, including Wikipedia dominance, possible pretraining contamination, mixed evidence for original visualizations, and evaluation using only one fine-tuned backbone.
weaknesses: The central visual-fidelity claim is not convincingly established. In the controlled comparison, original-image training clearly wins on only two tasks, matches on most others, and loses on one; the authors themselves note that the benchmarks largely do not test visual cues. The custom degradation score has no uncertainty analysis, normalizes by potentially small scores, and can reward stable but low absolute performance.

The held-out evaluation is not demonstrably leakage-free. Excluding task labels does not ensure unseen tables: MMTab structure tasks explicitly draw tables from sources such as InfoTabs, while InfoTabs is treated as held out. No global table-ID or near-duplicate audit across training and evaluation splits is reported, despite extensive overlap among the underlying Wikipedia datasets.

Comparisons confound dataset quality and diversity with scale and compute. TABLET-S/M/L contain approximately 0.69M/1.03M/3.42M training examples versus about 0.23M for MMTab and are all trained for three epochs. There is no matched-example or matched-update comparison for the general performance claims, while the larger mixed-image condition is also acknowledged as confounded by sample count.

The claim of state-of-the-art performance on 10 of 14 benchmarks is insufficiently supported. Main tables compare against a narrow set of Qwen/MMTab baselines rather than benchmark-specific prior systems, and appendix results show stronger open-weight models outperforming TABLET models on several tasks.

Dataset quality is not adequately validated. Retrieval uses a 0.70 string-similarity threshold and sometimes estimated crawl dates, but no human audit, matching precision, screenshot-completeness analysis, or label-noise estimate is reported. Presented examples themselves contain malformed or incomplete targets, suggesting inherited annotation noise.

Only one backbone is fine-tuned, apparently for one training seed; bootstrap resampling over test examples does not capture training variance. Decoding, output parsing, truncation rates, and the consequences of the very small 50,176-pixel input budget for large tables are also insufficiently documented or analyzed.

The data remain dominated by Wikipedia and PubTabNet, so claims about robustness to broadly diverse real-world tables exceed the demonstrated coverage of spreadsheets, enterprise documents, web applications, and other layouts.

As a large dataset release, the paper lacks a substantive discussion of licenses and redistribution compatibility across the 14 seed datasets, embedded images, privacy, harmful content, and takedown or maintenance procedures. Numerous count and terminology inconsistencies—such as 20 versus 21 tasks and conflicting Table Recognition test counts—also weaken confidence in curation rigor.
